documents.title: Guiding Principles for AI Use in Teaching (GenAI Teaching Guidelines)
documents.summary: The CTE's seven guiding principles for AI in teaching ask faculty to state AI rules in their syllabi, be open about their own AI use, verify AI output, protect student data and build AI literacy instead of policing use. It sets no university-wide student rule and leaves the decision to each instructor.
documents.stance_why: The document says 'faculty must convey in their course syllabi what is allowed or prohibited' and that 'Faculty and academic units are encouraged to adapt these guidelines'; it sets no AI rule for students itself and hands the choice to instructors, so delegates.

documents.summary: The Office of Student Conduct explains that AI misuse is handled under the existing Honor Code, with examples of cheating, plagiarism, falsification and complicity, a description of how cases are investigated, and sample syllabus statements in three categories. It leaves permission to instructors and tells students to ask.
documents.stance_why: The page says 'As the course instructor you may restrict and use Artificial Intelligence as you deem fit' and offers sample statements in three categories (no use, permitted in specific contexts, encouraged); it sets no single rule and the student 'is responsible for asking', so delegates with tiers.

units.why: The page says existing policies 'apply regardless of the tools used', so AI misuse is judged under the Honor Code; it classifies AI misuse as an integrity violation, P36 (P77 is the other candidate, but P36 matches the 'investigated and adjudicated' content).
